I can’t really let it go. It feels like they’re quietly tracking me and sending these little signals.\n\nDoctor: Have you had the feeling that your thoughts are being controlled or interfered with by someone else?\n\nPatient: Controlled? But that happens to people, right? Especially in my work, because if you miss one little detail with a client it can turn into a whole issue later. So… I’m not sure if that’s what you mean by interfered with. I haven’t really noticed someone else getting into my thoughts, no.\n\nDoctor: Do these thoughts about people sending you signals feel intrusive and unwanted, like they pop into your mind even when you don’t want them to?\n\nPatient: Yeah… I mean, sort of. It’s more like once something happens — like an invitation shows up after I’ve met with a client, or a panel topic lines up a little too neatly — I can’t stop turning it over.\n\nAnd I know, I know, people would say that’s just coincidence, especially here, because the arts people and the finance people overlap way more than you’d think. I was at this one event where the seating chart alone felt like someone was making a point, but then again those committees all talk to each other, so maybe—\n\nBut, yes, I guess they’re unwanted in the sense that I don’t want to spend my day thinking about it. I just can’t really let it go when it feels like certain people are quietly tracking who I’m meeting with and sending signals around it.\n\nDoctor: When these thoughts come up, do they feel to you like a real warning about what people are doing, or more like a thought your mind gets stuck on even though you suspect it may not be true?\n\nPatient: It feels like a warning at the time. That’s the hard part. I can tell myself afterward, okay, maybe this is just Cincinnati being small, people from the arts boards and the finance side all mixing together, same events, same donor lists—honestly those circles overlap in weird ways.\n\nBut when it happens, like an invitation shows up right after I’ve met with someone, or a panel topic sounds a little too close to something I was dealing with, or I get seated near somebody who connects back to a client… it doesn’t feel like just a thought I’m stuck on. Cincinnati’s smaller than people think—everybody knows everybody, especially if you go to enough fundraisers and networking things—but I just can’t really let it go. It keeps feeling intentional.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it’s possible that this feeling is mistaken, or are you certain those people are intentionally sending you signals?\n\nPatient: I mean… I know it could be mistaken, technically. I do tell myself that. Like, Cincinnati isn’t that big, and if you’re around the arts boards and finance people enough, you run into the same names, the same clients, the same gala committees.\n\nBut then something happens—like an invitation comes right after I meet with a certain client, or a panel topic feels too specific, or someone gets seated near me who… just shouldn’t be there by chance—and I’m back to thinking, no, this is intentional. I can’t really let it go. It feels like they’re quietly tracking me and sending these little signals.\n\nDoctor: Have you had the feeling that your thoughts are being controlled or interfered with by someone else?\n\nPatient: Controlled? I don’t… I don’t think I’d put it that way. Like, nobody’s steering my thoughts like a remote control or anything.\n\nSometimes I’ll get stuck on something, like a phrase from a meeting or the way someone said something at an event, and it’ll loop in my head longer than I want. It’s more like once something happens — like an invitation shows up after I’ve met with a client, or a panel topic lines up a little too neatly — I can’t stop turning it over.\n\nAnd I know, I know, people would say that’s just coincidence, especially here, because the arts people and the finance people overlap way more than you’d think. I was at this one event where the seating chart alone felt like someone was making a point, but then again those committees all talk to each other, so maybe—\n\nBut, yes, I guess they’re unwanted in the sense that I don’t want to spend my day thinking about it. I just can’t really let it go when it feels like certain people are quietly tracking who I’m meeting with and sending signals around it.\n\nDoctor: When these thoughts come up, do they feel to you like a real warning about what people are doing, or more like a thought your mind gets stuck on even though you suspect it may not be true?\n\nPatient: It feels like a warning at the time. That’s the hard part. I can tell myself afterward, okay, maybe this is just Cincinnati being small, people from the arts boards and the finance side all mixing together, same events, same donor lists—honestly those circles overlap in weird ways.\n\nBut when it happens, like an invitation shows up right after I’ve met with someone, or a panel topic sounds a little too close to something I was dealing with, or I get seated near somebody who connects back to a client… it doesn’t feel like just a thought I’m stuck on. It feels like they’re doing it on purpose, like they’re signaling that they know who I’m meeting with.\n\nAnd then later I’ll go back and forth with myself, but I can’t really shake it.\n\nDoctor: Have you heard or seen things that other people could not?\n\nPatient: I don’t think so. I mean, not like seeing a person standing there that nobody else sees, or hearing a voice talking to me when the room is quiet.\n\nSometimes at events, there’s so much noise—people talking over each other, music, the clinking glasses, you know—and I’ll think I heard my name or something about a client, but then it’s usually just… noise, or I can’t tell. That happens in crowded rooms. Those fundraisers are terrible for that, honestly, the acoustics are always bad.\n\nBut if you mean clear things other people couldn’t hear or see, no, I haven’t really noticed that.\n\nDoctor: Have other people told you that your speech is hard to follow or that you jump between ideas in a way that doesn’t make sense to them?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure. I mean, not usually? People sometimes tell me I’m giving too much background, but that’s different, I think. But I haven’t really had people say I’m jumping between ideas in a way that makes no sense.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been having this feeling that people are intentionally tracking you and sending you signals?\n\nPatient: It’s been… about two months, I think. Maybe a little more depending on where I start counting it, because at first it was just one or two odd coincidences and I didn’t really label it that way.\n\nBut the feeling that people are actually tracking my client meetings and sending little signals about it—that’s been around for roughly two months. But then I’ll see something—an invitation wording, who ends up near me, something that lines up with a meeting I had—and it comes back.\n\nSo I wouldn’t say there have been days where I’m totally free of it. Maybe moments where I can push it aside, but not gone.\n\nDoctor: Has this belief been present for longer than three months?\n\nPatient: No, not longer than three months. I’d put it at about two months… maybe a little around the edges, because I keep thinking back to when I first noticed things, like invitations or who was seated where, but the actual belief that my client meetings were being tracked and people were sending signals about it—about two months.\n\nDoctor: Since this started, have there been times when you felt very confused or puzzled about what was happening around you?\n\nPatient: Yeah… puzzled, definitely. Like, nobody’s steering my thoughts like a remote control or anything.\n\nSometimes I’ll get stuck on something, like a phrase from a meeting or the way someone said something at an event, and it’ll loop in my head longer than I want. But that happens to people, right? Especially in my work, because if you miss one little detail with a client it can turn into a whole issue later. So… I’m not sure if that’s what you mean by interfered with. I haven’t really noticed someone else getting into my thoughts, no.\n\nDoctor: Do these thoughts about people sending you signals feel intrusive and unwanted, like they pop into your mind even when you don’t want them to?\n\nPatient: Yeah… I mean, sort of. They don’t feel like random thoughts exactly, not like something silly popping in. It’s more like once something happens — like an invitation shows up after I’ve met with a client, or a panel topic lines up a little too neatly — I can’t stop turning it over.\n\nAnd I know, I know, people would say that’s just coincidence, especially here, because the arts people and the finance people overlap way more than you’d think. I was at this one event where the seating chart alone felt like someone was making a point, but then again those committees all talk to each other, so maybe—\n\nBut, yes, I guess they’re unwanted in the sense that I don’t want to spend my day thinking about it. I just can’t really let it go when it feels like certain people are quietly tracking who I’m meeting with and sending signals around it.\n\nDoctor: When these thoughts come up, do they feel to you like a real warning about what people are doing, or more like a thought your mind gets stuck on even though you suspect it may not be true?\n\nPatient: It feels like a warning at the time. It feels like they’re doing it on purpose, like they’re signaling that they know who I’m meeting with.\n\nAnd then later I’ll go back and forth with myself, but I can’t really shake it.\n\nDoctor: Have you heard or seen things that other people could not?\n\nPatient: I don’t think so. Some people want the headline first, and I’m more… I guess I build up to it.\n\nSo, hard to follow? Maybe occasionally, if I’m stressed or trying to explain too many pieces at once. But I haven’t really had people say I’m jumping between ideas in a way that makes no sense.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been having this feeling that people are intentionally tracking you and sending you signals?\n\nPatient: It’s been… about two months, I think. Maybe moments where I can push it aside, but not gone.\n\nDoctor: Has this belief been present for longer than three months?\n\nPatient: No, not longer than three months. I’d put it at about two months… maybe a little around the edges, because I keep thinking back to when I first noticed things, like invitations or who was seated where, but the actual belief that my client meetings were being tracked and people were sending signals about it—about two months.\n\nDoctor: Since this started, have there been times when you felt very confused or puzzled about what was happening around you?\n\nPatient: Yeah… puzzled, definitely. Why that wording? Why that person near me? So yes, I’ve felt pretty puzzled by it. That’s kind of why I came in, because I can’t sort it out or just let it go.\n\nDoctor: Since this started, have the people close to you noticed a big change in how you’ve been acting day to day?\n\nPatient: Yeah… a little, I think. My mind jumps around anyway, especially when I’m stressed.\n\nSo… no, I haven’t really felt like thoughts were being inserted into my head.\n\nDoctor: Have you felt that outside forces were controlling your actions or movements?\n\nPatient: No, I don’t think so.
